utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please sit down. I thank you, and good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and my learned friends from the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Patricia Sellers, co-counsel, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. I appear for Mr. Naser Oric together with Mr. John Jones. Joining us today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. Yesterday I was put on alert, and I put the Defence on alert, thinking that they had already been -- in fact, they should have been alerted that there would be a legal point, a legal matter to be raised by the Prosecution in relation to the recalling of a witness, a particular witness, Mr. Eric. I take it that by now you would have prepared yourselves on this point. I take it that there is also no ad hoc formal written motion, that this is going to be submitted orally and dealt with orally, and later on, another day or some other day, will be decided on orally by the Trial Chamber. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We discussed it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you please tell me who from the Prosecution bench is going to address the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I requested Ms. Patricia Sellers to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers. Can I ask you to finish in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Possibly sooner than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the argument requires more than that, otherwise I would have said 15 minutes. But I think in five minutes either side -- you can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also to our learned friends. If we understand the issue correctly, it's basically in response to the Trial Chamber's request yesterday, with respect to whether Mr. Eric should be called back for the purpose of direct-examination, cross-examination, or solely for cross-examination. In that sense, the Prosecution will present very succinct arguments asking the Trial Chamber to please ask Mr. Eric to be allowed to be led on examination, and subsequently on cross-examination, and I would state from the outset that we are quite affair and have read Your Honours' decision concerning this, and we understand that the decision appears to be limited to calling Mr. Eric back for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was only one motion, Ms. Sellers, and that was a Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. And I understand that we would at this point in time respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to reconsider only the holding in terms of limitation on cross-examination. The Prosecution's basic arguments are that the Trial Chamber did not find any fault or negligence on behalf of the Prosecution when we discovered the Kravica video. It was quite well noted in both the decision and in our oral discussion here in the chamber that this video had been searched for prior to the start of this trial, that we assured the Trial Chamber that we would be diligent in looking for it, and I think the Trial Chamber was satisfied with that. So we arrived basically at the moment as to Mr. Eric will be called back, but only what will be the scope of his examination. The Prosecution submits that Mr. Eric, because he will now be having new evidence put before him, or evidence that has come to light that neither the Prosecution nor the Defence will during their period of direct examination or cross-examination, should therefore be allowed to be led on direct with this new evidence arising from the video, and not just in cross-examination. That is within the holding of jurisprudence from this Tribunal. And I will briefly cite to the Galic decision, where the situation was quite similar. New evidence came forward that neither the Prosecution nor the Defence counsel had a chance to directly ask the witness about, and therefore the witness was called back. I would cite that the Galic decision is found in decision on admission into evidence of Dr. Vilmos Kovac's expert report, and the date on that is the 2nd of August, 2002. If I could just very briefly explain the factual situation that gave rise to the situation in Galic. It appears that an expert report had been prepared, but it had been a draft report. When both the Defence and the Prosecution called the expert witness, Mr. Vilmos Kovac, they did -- noted that the Defence had found discrepancies between the translation and the original report. They requested that the witness be recalled to explain the circumstances in which that report was given. In addition, when a final report was put forward, there were two additional pages. The additional pages recommended new evidence that neither the Defence nor the Prosecution had seen and had a chance to question the expert on either in their direct examination or in their cross-examination. So therefore the witness was recalled. He was examined first by the Prosecution and then cross-examined by the Defence. The Defence was further allowed to examine the witness on the history of the statement and on certain particulars as new evidence. Therefore, we would state that this Galic case is very much the similar situation that we have with the Kravica videotape. I would just very briefly like to distinguish the Galic case in our present factual circumstances from the case of Furundzija, where a witness was called back --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if my learned friend is going to rely on -- on case law, and I'm somewhat dismayed that she is because we had an informal agreement that we weren't going to cite case law in this argument. But at least we have copies so we can follow. Because I certainly can't follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are easily available, Mr. Jones. Perhaps you can get one of your assistants --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're not able to connect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I will -- excuse me, I will certainly give cites. The copy I have now is marked up, but we will give you copies and -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I won't be in a position to respond as to the case law without copies of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. If case law is being up in the discussion, then obviously you're entitled to -- on the other hand, I am aware that there isn't much case law on this issue. It's not an incident which is the first time that it's being raised, and you even find the similar incidents dealt with in standard procedural textbooks on English common law, anyway, and even Scottish procedural law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I simply won't be able to respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is much to say, to be honest with you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, if I may continue. I do agree with you, there is not a wealth of case law from the Tribunal. I would just cite two -- two other cases where the -- a similar appeared to be raised, but I would like to distinguish that issue from the facts that we have before us. And one is the Furundzija case, where the case was reopened. That was basically based --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speaker kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. That was based upon an inquiry of Rule 68 material. The distinguishing point is that that Rule 68 material, the Trial Chamber held, was known to the Prosecution, therefore Prosecution, having known that material, could have raised it on its direct examination. So, therefore, the witness was recalled but only for the purposes of the cross-examination on material evidence they did not have before them during their cross-examination. And again, I need not tell Your Honours, there was a slightly similar situation in the Brdjanin case that called for re-opening the case of the Prosecutor and there the Trial Chamber did not allow that one rebuttal. The distinguishing points are that when there is evidence that is new to both the Prosecution and to the Defence attorney, the right for examination and for cross-examination should be reviewed and respected, hopefully, by this Trial Chamber. Where that information or that evidence was not new and therefore the Prosecution could have led on it, then it appears that the Trial Chamber limits the call -- calling the witness back to cross-examination. My last point on this argument is just, Your Honours, I think that we're certainly aware of what has become an often-quoted holding within our Tribunal that a fair trial must be fair both to the Prosecution and to the Defence, and we would state, and I believe that is just slightly, if I can quote the jurisprudence, that does come from Aleksovski, that the Trial Chamber look at the issues of equity that necessarily need to be visited in this situation so that we might be able to look at the new evidence, ask few questions limited to that new evidence, not to reopen a direct examination in its totality, and that the Defence then can cross-examine, limiting their cross-examination to the new evidence. And in that manner, we feel that a fair trial will be held certainly for the accused, Mr. Oric, but also for the Prosecutor. Your Honour, those are basically the gist of my arguments, and I am certainly more than willing to provide Defence counsel with pertinent but, I will say, very limited jurisprudence on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can be very brief. I can summarise my submissions really in four points. The first is, and my starting point is, Your Honours' decision, which is that Mr. Eric be called to reappear before the Trial Chamber for further cross-examination. Now, if I understand my learned friend correctly, she's now also asking the Chamber to reconsider the decision. In my submission, that's beyond the parameters of this debate and possibly beyond the parameters of what Your Honours can do in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this up straight away. The Trial Chamber - I think I can speak for the other two Judges as well - the way I see it at the present moment is you're correct, what we dealt with was a request on the part of the Defence to recall Eric for a further cross-examination. There was no demand at the time, no request at the time, on the part of the Prosecution to recall Mr. Eric in the wake of the discovery or rediscovery of this video. However, following our decisions, the Prosecution has now basically tabled a motion orally to have also Mr. Eric examined in direct before he is actually cross-examined, as per our previous decision. This is basically -- in other words, you are now facing a demand or a request on the part of the Prosecution to have Mr. Eric examined in direct, apart from being cross-examined. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I merely note that it's moved from a housekeeping matter to do with proofing to a new motion on which Your Honours are going to have to rule. There is authority, and as I say, there was an informal agreement that we wouldn't cite authority so I haven't prepared authority, but I know there is authority that motions to reconsider are not part of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Unfortunately, I can't provide that authority to Your Honours. As far as the authority put forward by my learned friend is concerned, as I say, I simply do not have copies of those authorities and I'm not in a position to respond. But I start from the point of view that, as things stand, Mr. Eric is coming back for cross-examination. As I understand it, proofing is for direct examination, and so, in our submission, there is no question of him being proofed again, because he's not going to be -- he's not going to be examined in chief, and In our submission, he shouldn't be examined in chief. In fact, in our submission, it's really -- the position should be treated as if Mr. Eric was still within the precincts of the Tribunal, halfway through his testimony, and there should be no contact from the side of the Prosecutor with Mr. Eric. It should simply be a question of the Registry informing him that he should be brought back for cross-examination. We say that because - and this comes to my second point - this isn't new material. The Prosecution has had this material. It hasn't just come to light or it doesn't constitute new evidence. The Prosecutor had it. The fact that they -- that Your Honours may have found that they're not so to blame in not disclosing it to us doesn't mean that it's new and it's fallen from the sky. They did have it and if as a result of their own fault they didn't find it, then that's a matter for them. Finally, I would simply say that my learned friend has referred to a fair trial being also fair to the Prosecution. Well, the Prosecution bring the case, and they have to bring it fairly. The accused didn't ask to be indicted and brought before this Tribunal. The Prosecution indicted him and so it's for them and for Your Honours to ensure a fair trial. So frankly, a fair trial for the Prosecutor, I don't know what that means. It's a fair trial for the accused and that's what Your Honours should be concerned to ensure. In our submission, the motion should be refused that he be -- that Mr. Eric should be examined in chief. There should be no contact between the Prosecution and Mr. Eric. All contact should be through the Registry. And in that regard, I just wish to state that I hope the Prosecution haven't contacted Mr. Eric yet, because, of course, that's a matter which is to be regulated today. And even a telephone conversation could constitute a form of proofing. So I certainly hope that there has been no contact. In our submission, there should be no contact. He should be brought here and cross-examined by us, and then the Prosecution can re-examine him. Unless I can assist you further, Your Honour, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further remarks, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the briefest of rebuttal remarks would just be that while that videotape was in the Office of the Prosecutor, the Prosecution, during the proofing of Mr. Eric before, did not have access to it. That was among the time periods that we were desperately trying to locate the video. So he was not proofed on that. I would just like to limit our actions today to say that we're talking about examination and cross-examination and we're really not talking about, at this point in time, issues of proofing. Proofing goes if examination is granted. And then also, just to assure Your Honours -- and this I would say would be outside the scope of my argument, I don't find it at this point necessarily relevant -- but to assure Your Honours that we have certainly not had any contact with Mr. Eric since this decision, I will say that when Mr. Eric was dismissed as a witness from this court, that we did go back, thank him for his testimony, shake his hand, ask him how he was, and as we usually do to witnesses, as he was on his way back to his homeland. So if does say that "I've had contact with the Prosecutor after I left the Trial Chamber," that might be the contact he's referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would add just one point, Your Honour, and I apologise for overlooking it. I also just wish to say that in opposing our motion, the Prosecution submitted that in fact the video raised nothing new and that therefore there was no need for him to be cross-examined upon it. In light of that position, it seems inappropriate for the Prosecution to consider that there are new matters which they need to proof Mr. Eric on, matters which they need to examine him in chief upon, because their position is that the video doesn't raise any new matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say on this, Ms. Sellers, because undoubtedly whoever it was the view, I can't remember, did say that -- I think it was Mr. Wubben -- there was nothing new in this. I don't know, I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was the position of the Prosecution at the time. We basically thought that the issue that the Defence was raising was going to be limited to the issue of whether he was wearing a uniform on the 7th or not, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, the rest was discussed too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And then after the rest was discussed during the course of Mr. Di Fazio's argument. Seeing the extent to which the Defence now would like to cross-examine him on other issues beyond the scope of the possible -- the date of the video and the wearing of the uniform, the Prosecution's position now has modified and we would like to be able to examine him on those other attendant issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've heard enough. We will reserve our position, and we will decide at some later point in time -- at some later point in time. Do you have an idea in your mind, at least, when Mr. Eric will be recalled? Have you, in other words, tried to fit him in any schedule that you may have been working upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. So far, but only provisionally and tentative, in the second week of December, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second week of December is next --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, that's from now two weeks. I know that's on short notice. That's why I inform you that it is tentative and provisional. But just to give a follow-up action to what has been the latest developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Any further preliminaries before we bring in the witness? Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe prior to bringing in this witness we possibly need to go into private session for the issues of witness protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, and to inform the public, the Trial Chamber was in private session for a while interviewing the next witness in order to be able to decide upon a Prosecution motion for protective measures to be put in place relative to this witness, and the response of the Defence which opposed the protective measures being sought by the Prosecution. The protective measures sought by the Prosecution were the following: Pseudonym, facial and voice distortion. The Trial Chamber, during a short break, deliberated on this, and by a majority vote, Judge Brydensholt dissenting, we have come to the conclusion that out of the three protective measures sought by Defence, considering the special circumstances attached to the witness's case, and with the caveat that this will not, however, constitute a precedent for future reference in this or in any other case, we've come to the conclusion to grant only facial distortion but no pseudonym and no voice distortion. That is the position. We will now bring in the witness. I think we need to go into private session while the witness walks through -- walks inside the courtroom and sits -- takes his chair. I will explain to him, and then we can proceed. It's not necessary because we are in courtroom II, I take it. Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that the technicians know that there will be facial distortion. So now please remain standing. We have taken a decision, and the decision we have taken is that, given the special circumstances that you have explained to us, which, under normal circumstances, would not entitle anyone, would not entitle anyone to protective measures; however, we want you to feel at ease while you are giving evidence, and by a majority vote, we have decided to grant you only facial distortion. But we are not going to hide your name and we are not going to hide your voice. What the public will not see is your face. And that should put your mind, at least, at ease that the most important protective measure has been granted to you. But we honestly cannot even, for a while, entertain granting you the other two protective measures, because we would be opening doors which we would then not be able to close later on. I hope that satisfies you. Before you start giving evidence -- by the way, if you look down at the monitor, you will see how the other people are going to see you. If you look at the monitor, that's how you're going to look to others. In other words, I would assume that most persons outside of your village do not know you by name; the Muslims you work for do not know you by name. And not seeing your face, they wouldn't be able to -- but that's the utmost that we can grant. Before you start giving evidence, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is being handed to you by Madam Usher. Please take that text in your -- that piece of paper in your hand, read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's going to happen now is Ms. Sellers is going to ask you a series of questions. I don't think the direct will last long, having gone through your statement. And then you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: appearing for Mr. Oric. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness might exceed the one and a half hour time period; therefore, I would ask that I may be allowed to lead him on several parts of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, that are pertinent more so to background facts of the events that led up and transpired in relationship to the allegations in the indictment that take place in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask that you state your name for the record, and to tell the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Slavoljub Rankic. I was born on the 26th of March, 1951, in the village of Sikiric, the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is your father's name Nedeljko [phoen], or Nedji [phoen] For short?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Nedeljko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Rankic, were you married, and were you the father of daughters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I am married and I do have two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, did you work in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, before 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you work in a company where close relatives of the accused, Mr. Oric, were employed? You have to say an answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. One man's name was Oric Ramiz and the other was Oric Jusuf, and we worked together in the construction company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you have good relationships with these relatives of Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Very good, and for a long time. And I'm still on good terms with Jusuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, did you live in the village of Bjelovac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, yes, I did, I lived in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is the village of Bjelovac located on the banks of the Drina River in the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, don't most people who lived in the village of Bjelovac live at the foot of a stretch of a -- stretch of mountains that then leads to the banks of the river?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about how many villagers lived in Bjelovac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: The total number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Over 100 households.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would that be about 500 or 600 inhabitants in Bjelovac at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, across the Drina River, in front of Bjelovac, does the town of Grabovica in Serbia exist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, I'm going to take you through a series of questions basically to describe the geographical location, if Your Honours will indulge me, and then I'll ask for an exhibit of a map to be put forward on the ELMO. Behind the town of Bjelovac, is there a mountain chain that eventually leads into a mine that's referred to as the Sase mine?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was that mine the major employer of the village and the surrounding area of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did some of the people who worked in the Sase mine live across the Drina River in what is now Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: There are some like that as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In Bjelovac, was there also a water factory or a water plant that was located and supplied water to the surrounding regions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In the town of Bjelovac, was there also a water factory or a water plant --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right, a water plant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And from this water plant, did water pipes run from Bjelovac to the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, going across Zaluzje, Plojavica [phoen] up to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And weren't these water pipes among the major suppliers of water to that town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the main supplier, but yes, it was used a lot. There was a reserve pipeline, but this was actually the main one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Other than the mine and the water plant, did people in Bjelovac, in 1992 or just before, also make their living by working in the towns of either Srebrenica or Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Therefore, is it correct to say that Bjelovac was not predominantly an agricultural community?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the inhabitants of Bjelovac basically derive their livelihood through salaries, through employment, and not through raising crops, then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, people did that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to the south of Bjelovac, is there a village called Sikirici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Sikiric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sikiric, excuse me my pronunciation. And was Sikiric divided into two sections, Gornji Sikiric, being the upper part, and Donji Sikiric, being the lower part?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, to the north of the village of Bjelovac, is that where the town of Bratunac is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, is there a major transport road running from the town of Bratunac through Bjelovac and that continues down to Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To the north of Bjelovac, in between Bjelovac and Bratunac, is there a village called Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And further from Zaluzje, also to the north of Bjelovac but prior to arriving at Bratunac, is there a village called Voljevica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, there is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to the south -- actually, the southwest of Sikiric, is there a town called Pirici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like at this point to give the witness exhibit -- a map that we'll use as our first exhibit today. Could I ask Madam Usher to supply the witness with a red pen, or one that he can use.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask the witness to please mark the following locations that you've just testified about on the map. Would you please draw a circle around the town of Bjelovac for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I don't believe that the pen shows up very well. Is that okay for Your Honours, or would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I can only follow to what I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, I can only follow through what I'm seeing on the monitor. Having it zoomed in, I can detect a circle. But I had heard you say a red -- is it red? Because I'm not seeing any red on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It looks as if it's a red pen. Might I suggest if we can see this will make a better visual for the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the circle would be around the entire word, Bjelovac, not just the first three letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now could you please mark for the Trial Chamber on the map where Bratunac is.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you also mark for Your Honours the town of Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Would you now mark on the map the road that runs from Bratunac through Bjelovac to Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness, the town of Bratunac, Bjelovac, and Sikiric that you have just marked, are they predominantly Bosnian Serb towns or Bosnian Muslim towns, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: It was inhabited by both the Muslims and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And specifically in the town of Bjelovac, what was the percentage of Muslims that lived in Bjelovac and the percentage of Serbs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was roughly -- I'm not a statistical expert, but I would say 10 per cent -- well, I knew the names of the families. One family was named Berzadic, the other one was Sinanovic. The third family's surname was Dalbasic, and the fourth family was called Sokolic, or something like that. But they were the four families who lived in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is Sikiric a predominantly Muslim town, or was it a Bosnian Serb town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs, and several Muslim families as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now indicate on the map where is the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you now indicate the town of Grabovica, that is on -- in front of Bjelovac, on the other side of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you to mark on -- the following locations on the map that you've testified about. Would you please put a circle around Pirici.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And now would you put a circle around Zaluzje.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then I will lastly ask you to put a circle around Voljevica.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these towns, Pirici, Zaluzje, Voljevica, are these predominantly Bosnian Muslim villages or Bosnian Serb villages, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They were inhabited 100 per cent by Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in addition to the villages that you've described, do the inhabitants in this region of -- near the Drina River also identify their location by the proximity or their closeness to four streams or brooks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there was Vrnecka Rijeka, Bijelovacka Rijeka, Loznicka Rijeka, and Tegarska [phoen]. That was the division, how the villages were divided between the rivers, from one river to the next. And the distance, I'm not going to be exact, but it was between one and a half and two kilometres in between, in between the rivers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So all the people might have lived in a town, a location, such as Sikiric, they might say -- they might identify themselves as being from an area named by the brook and not named by the town; is that correct, Mr. Rankic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, they're small hamlets, settlements, be it Loznicka Rijeka, that river or brook, and that, it was called Loznicka Rijeka, whereas across the river was Sikiric. But they were all very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you be asking the witness to mark any further towns or villages on this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as a matter of fact, throughout his testimony, I would like to have the map stay next to him, and there will be a couple other markations. Now, I don't know for purposes of looking on the monitor whether it's helpful to possibly change colours, or is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it will help us monitor-wise, because I think all the colours are neutral on the monitor, on the video. But the purpose -- why I asked the question was that I would like to enter for the record that the witness has, until now, marked on the map, which is soon going to be admitted as Prosecution Exhibit number -- registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P450, all the towns and villages that were indicated to him by the Prosecution. This could be confirmed by the Trial Chamber who has been following on the monitor the markings put on this document by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, turning your attention to the spring of 1992, I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber certain events or provocations that might have happened between April and June that caused tension between the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Serbs that live in the region that you've just described and illustrated on the map.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: There weren't any great tensions, but as of May, some tensions were felt. The Muslims that lived in Bjelovac left and went to the villages of Pirici, Zaluzje, and so on, because they had relatives there. And that's when you could feel the tension. They didn't want to go back to their villages so as not to collect up information or anything about any sabotage or anything like that. But then we placed village watches or guards around the village. They were in the forest, in the woods, and they provoked us. But they didn't jeopardise anybody's lives, they just provoked them. And that's why we set up the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I couldn't follow --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm going to go back with specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, because there is something that doesn't click here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, when you were that "they were in the woods," are you referring to Bosnian Muslims or are you referring to village guards who provoked you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims were provoking us, because they weren't able to go to their houses, they couldn't get to their houses. That's why they provoked us from those woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I see. Now, you said the Muslims left Bjelovac in the spring of 1992. Did they leave as a result of armed violence among the villagers in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. They were afraid. But otherwise there was no violence. They were afraid for their own safety and security. And of course their relatives exerted pressure that they should move out, the relatives from these other villages exerted pressure on them to move out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether there was an attack in the part of Sikirici, that was Gornji Sikiric, in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know who attacked Gornji Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Gornji Sikiric was attacked by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And who told you that Gornji Sikiric was attacked by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, my father lived in Gornji Sikiric, and he came to live with me because he was expelled from Sikiric. There was an attack. A woman was killed during the attack. I think her name was Milja Prodanovic. And the other villagers fled to Donja Sikiric, so Gornji Sikiric was empty and remained up there. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know if during the attack on Gornji Sikiric that there was burning and looting by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happened. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the Bosnian Muslims that left Gornji Sikiric, did they come to stay in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In 1992, after the attack that you've testified about in Gornji Sikiric, did the Bosnian - I'm sorry, the Bosnian Serbs - come to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did. I understand now. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were they considered refugees in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, I took my father into my own house, whereas the others went to the school building. And that's where they were put up. People who didn't have relatives there, they were put up in the school, and that's where they spent their days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know if there was an attack on the village of Loznica in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was on Vidovdan, St. Vitus Day, the St. Vitus holiday in June. And the Muslims attacked the village of Loznica on that day and killed eight people and wounded 16 others. The other people who survived moved to Bjelovac, and we put them up in the school building there as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, during that Muslim attack on Loznica, was there burning and looting of the homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's what eyewitnesses said. As soon as the Serbs left the village, the looting began straight away. But usually what was taken was food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you turn back to the map that is to your right, and I would like you to indicate for the Trial Chamber where is Loznica on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Across from Pirici. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you indicate that on the map with a marker?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I see, yes. Thank you. Now we'll go back to testimony. After the attacks on Loznica and Gornji Sikiric, was the area, the mountains behind Bjelovac, particularly in that area of Gornji Sikirici and Loznica, in the hands of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the area to the north of Bratunac, the towns that you've mentioned before, the villages you've mentioned before, Zaluzje, Voljevica, were they in the hands of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, could you explain: During that time period, was it safe to travel on the road between Bjelovac and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: In May it was safe. May, May was safe, no provocations. You could go from Bjelovac to Bratunac and back. But in June the provocations started, ambushes and so on, so it was no longer safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who was conducting the am bushes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: The Muslim forces, in the area of Zaluzje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. It's just a question on the transcript and some confusion. First of all, we had a reference to villages north of Bratunac, which I think has to be wrong in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that's north of Bjelovac. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Secondly, the witness didn't say "yes," he made a sound but it certainly wasn't a yes. That was a blank and it became yes subsequently. Because as I heard it, he didn't actually give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have doubt on that, I will do that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to read again the question that was put to you, changing the word Bratunac for Bjelovac, or the other way around, and then I will ask you to answer that question again. Was the area to the north of Bjelovac, the towns that you have mentioned before, the villages you've mentioned before, Zaluzje, Voljevica, were they in the hands of the Bosnian Muslims? What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could we have a date for that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In 1992, we're talking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The road from Bjelovac to Bratunac was free in May. You could move around. But in June, the Muslims had taken over, taken control of that road, that line of communication. And they set up ambushes. There were casualties, and we were no longer able to use that road any more for our own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you haven't answered the question I put to you, which was to try and clear up the previous answer, because two mistakes had been made there. These towns or villages, Zaluzje, Voljevica, were in the hands of the -- were they in the hands of the Bosnian Muslims? And if they were, which period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From June it was in their hands, so we weren't allowed to pass that way, because there were ambushes there all the time so you couldn't pass that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that answers the question now. Yes, Ms. Sellers, you can proceed, please. Thank you, Mr. Jones, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, because of these events that you described, the sniping, the attacks on certain Bosnian Serb villages, and the refugee population, did there come a time period, therefore, in the spring of 1992 when the villagers in Bjelovac organised a village guard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber how the village guard was organised and how it operated then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning we stood guard in front of our houses, each person in front of his own house. Later on we pooled our forces and had several houses to one guard. So, for example, this evening, there would be two of us from these houses and the next day two other men from some other houses, so we would gain in time. That's how we organised the village watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: About how many persons participated in the village guard in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We had 15 guard posts from Bjelovac and counting Sikiric, as far as I know. Fifteen guard posts, places where we stood guard. Some of these posts were manned sometimes by four men, five men. I can't explain exactly why and how.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And how many shifts were there in this guard -- in this posting in the village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: As it was summertime, we did it this way: Up until 12, one shift, and then from midnight to the morning, the second shift. The younger people would stand guard up to midnight because they liked to sleep, so we placed the older people on guard from midnight to the morning, because they couldn't sleep very well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: -- anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- you stated you were guarding. In which way were you guarding, facing the Drina River or facing the mountains behind you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We stood guard in the direction of the forest, because that's where the provocation came from, from the forested area. So we wanted to protect that side. We didn't expect an attack to come from the Drina River side. So that was our strategy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time period when women participated in the village guard as well as men?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. No. Only men. Only men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did any of the women guard their houses, then, as private individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We used women only to clean the school building and to prepare food for the refugees and for hygiene. That's what the women did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was there a commander of the village guard who assisted you in organising the different shifts of the different men that participated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber his name.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a man named Milisav who was in charge of all our guards. We would report to him, that kind of thing. The name was Milisav Ilic. He was responsible for the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also did --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: There was a rotation system, but he is one commander that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as village guards, did you receive uniforms? Did you receive uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes and no. Those who had uniforms from before, who were reserve officers with the former JNA, not camouflage uniforms, just plain, regular, standard-issue uniforms, they used those. But all the other people were just wearing plain clothes, as farmers do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did your village guard have contact with people in Bratunac, the Bratunac Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the nature of your contact with the Bratunac Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was for food supplies, food and ammunition for defending the village, and some other necessities which I can't be very specific about right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the ammunition for protecting the village, was that also ammunition so that you could go out and attack other villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you -- did the village guard attack other villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I ask at what file you are talking the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're taking the break at the usual time, at a quarter to 4. You have two or three minutes left, unless you prefer to stop now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would prefer to stop now. I have a -- certain areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Sellers. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from. More or less, Mr. Jones, how much time do you think you require for your cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's hard to say because the direct-examination is lasting a lot longer than we thought. Perhaps two hours. I think we won't finish with this witness today at this rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. I may force you to. We'll have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How much more time do you require, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would hope to finish within this time segment. We have a couple other questions, and then we would like to move the situation of the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And tomorrow we have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, there is another Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you had indicated that you would finish this witness in two hours. This is the time that you had indicated for this witness, two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. But I think this morning we have had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I'm fully aware of that. I'm fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's why we'll try to finish this as rapidly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to finish as rapidly as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, you mentioned -- you testified that the TO brought food supplies down to the town of Bjelovac. This was in the summer of 1992, I believe we're speaking about June. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber: Were you still working in Srebrenica in June, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And had the workers from the mine in Sase stopped receiving their pay by this time in June 1992, those who lived in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to answer yes or no, not just nod with your head, because we -- the translators have to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was it also impossible for the workers to go from Srebrenica to Bratunac to receive their salaries at this time, in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So isn't it the case that the TO in Bratunac supplied food to the villagers of Bjelovac and also to the refugees that had come into Bjelovac by the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was the food that was supplied to Bjelovac by the TO, was that used to feed VRS soldiers who were stationed in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We received flour, oil, and sugar, the families did. And they had a kitchen, the refugees. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any VRS soldiers stationed in the town of Bjelovac in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. Only the escort for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, is the convoy that you're referring to the convoy that would bring food down from Bratunac to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did a Mr. Deronjic from Bratunac ever come to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what he did in Bjelovac when he came down?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: He promised the local population that they would be safe; they would be provided assistance in terms of food, that sort of thing. He made lots of promises.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did he ever station troops in Bjelovac to protect the town, then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes, he did, while the attacks were frequent, and then the attacks ceased and he withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did there come a time in June 1992 when the water pipes that led from Bjelovac to Bratunac were sabotaged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, which forces or who sabotaged those water pipelines?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: On the road between Bjelovac and Bratunac, the Muslim forces did that. They blew the pipes up, and there was no water supply for Bratunac. Ever since, convoys to Bjelovac became less and less frequent because they didn't need to go there and protect the water supply system there. That's how we were eventually left to our own devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you're referring to the convoys from Bratunac to Bjelovac, you're referring to the TO convoys from Bratunac; is that correct, Mr. Rankic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your attention to the summer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Before you do, how does he know that it was the Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that blew up the pipes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please answer His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How could you be so sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that there were frequent ambushes by the Muslim forces, and that's why we assumed that it had been them. There was no one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's an assumption, basically. You are assuming because you can't think of anyone else; is that the correct way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't know. I'm hardly sufficiently educated to interpret that. It was my assumption that it was the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, do you know whether the Bosnian Serb forces or the Bratunac TO blew up the water pipes that led between Bjelovac and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I know they came there to carry out repairs, but they would mend those and they would go back. So at one point it became impossible to carry out any further repairs. I don't think they would have done that. There was a lot of people in Bratunac who were left without water.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn your attention to a period between June 1992 and December 1992. Was there a fear in the town of -- in the village of Bjelovac of a possible attack from the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know the person from Bjelovac during that time period who was taken prisoner in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was that person a Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: It was a young man, aged 14. He was captured Srebrenica. And there was an exchange at the yellow bridge, Zuti Most. He was exchanged and he came to Bjelovac. His uncle was Milan Petrovic, and he then stayed with him. He was the one who told us that back in Srebrenica there was a man named Naser, because at the time we didn't know who he was. Later on his boys called him Naser, so Naser became his nickname. His name was Slobodan Petrovic, and that was the nickname he got from the young boys his own age who teased him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was he captured by members of Bosnian Muslim forces, this young man?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said, and that's how he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During the summer of 1992, did the village guard continue to guard the village, looking toward the mountains?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was Bjelovac ever attacked in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No, not a big attack. There were acts of provocation in the evening hours. It went on for 15 minutes and then stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to December 1992, and was there an attack on Bjelovac at that time period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Could I draw your attention to December of 1992, and ask you: Was there an attack on Bjelovac at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Between the 1st and the 14th of December, it was quiet, no incidents. It was so quiet, in fact, that we realised the war was over. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, then, what happened on the 14th of December, after this period you've just described, the 1st to the 14th, where it was quiet.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Until the 14th of December, it had been very peaceful. I was standing guard that evening, between 1800 and 2400 hours. There were no signs of an immediate attack. Everything was quiet, and that was the report I gave to the person who relieved me. I went to bed. Everything was quiet. At a quarter past six, suddenly there were sounds of shooting, heavy shooting. I got up. I didn't believe what was happening. I came out. There was no shooting near my house, but at Loznicka Rijeka, you could hear bursts of gunfire, heavy gunfire. While I was there, one of my neighbours, Dara Filipovic, came over. She told me, "The Muslims are coming." They're shooting from the direction of the Drina River. I said, That's impossible. We never received any word from any of the guards that we were about to come under attack. And she said, My husband left the house and headed towards the field toilet, and he was killed right there. I couldn't believe my own eyes. When I left the house, I saw two or three soldiers there. They were shooting at me. I ran towards the house, and she was shot in her right foot. I gave her first aid, and I took her back to my house. So that was the first I saw of the attack. A while later, another neighbour named Stevka, aged 65, came to us to seek help. We were there expecting something, that something would happen. We didn't know what. She said, My son had been wounded. He left to feed the pigs that were near the Drina River. There was a barn there, a shed they had. Milun went off to help, as well as Novak Husic, and they left. However, when they found this man named Bozo Todorovic, they pulled him out. They came to the house, 3 or 4 metres from the house, and the same soldiers that were there fired at the people who were trying to pull out. They killed Milun and wounded Novak and the mother, Stevka Todorovic. I approached them and I saw that they had been wounded. Stevka was wounded in the chest, and Novak was wounded in the kidneys. I took them back to my house. I didn't know what to do, so I gave them water to drink and they stayed in my house. There was heavy shooting, and my windows were smashed. I could no longer keep the wounded persons inside the room, but I brought them out into the corridor. It was safer there because there were no windows. I was in the corridor, and I left the house again to see what was going on. There was a lull, there was no longer any shooting. To the left of my house, towards the Drina River, I observed smoke rising. I was not able to tell exactly what the reason was, what caused the smoke, so I went up to the first floor in order to get a better view. From a first-floor window of my house, I realised that Nikola Petrovic's house was on fire. Around his house there was a group of people, maybe about 10 people, I can't believe be very specific, but they were capering about near his house, making faces. I stayed there for about 10 minutes. I was not being shot at at the time, but I heard shouts and yells around the house. And I noticed that there was a man calling out the name Suljo and another name, Mirsad. And this man named Suljo was very gruff with this other man named Mirsad. It wasn't very easy for me to understand exactly what was going on, but that's all I saw. To the right of where I was standing, there was smoke rising from Jovanovici, which is another village about 400 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to ask you a couple questions about what you've just described to the Trial Chamber. When you first went out of your house, you testified that you ran into a neighbour, Dara, who was explaining about her husband. Did she tell you about whether her husband had a gun and was firing his weapon at the any of the people who attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: He was wearing his pyjamas. It was a quarter past six in the morning, and he needed to see a man about a dog. And there was a field toilet, so he went there. He was only wearing his pyjamas. That's what she told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, did she tell you whether he was shooting at anyone at that time period or attacking anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You've also spoken about people --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. No. That's at least what she told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. You've also spoken about people named Milun, Novak, who were assisting someone called Bozo. Were they carrying weapons and shooting at the attackers at that time period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. There was no way that they could, because they couldn't even see him. He was behind the barns that were there. They couldn't have noticed him. They didn't know that he was there. It was a mistake. We didn't expect an attack to come from the direction of the Drina River. We were greatly surprised, and so were many other people. That's why there were so many victims. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you yourself, did you have a gun and were you shooting at the attackers at this time period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I did have a weapon, but I didn't make a sound. I did not want to disclose my position, because that would have made me a target.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you went to the first floor of your house. The first floor of your house, does that give you a view of other houses or surrounding areas from your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you say the first floor, is that the floor above the ground floor where you enter into your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were people capering about. Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber what these people who were capering about were wearing.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is something I forgot. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They had backpacks on their backs and some bandanas around their heads. As far as I could tell, the bandanas were orange. These people were moving about Nikola's house, moving back and forth, carrying weapons, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. And as they were moving around Nikola's house with their weapons, did anything happen to Nikola's house at that time period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Nikola's house was on fire, and they were near the house. There was smoke rising, and that was the first house in my village that was set fire to, because it was near the Drina River. It was the house that was the closest to the river in our village. And all the other houses in the village were by the roadside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, were these people who were dressed in that manner, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, which ones?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume soldiers. Their moves were quick.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did their actions appear to be coordinated and very efficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of a question that is. I don't know what that means, were their actions -- is my learned friend referring to their physical coordination or what precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's self-explanatory. If the witness has problems with understanding it, particularly since the words have to be translated, interpreted in his own language, then I will intervene. But you and I should understand what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So far they're simply capering. I don't know who they are coordinating with or who they are supposed to be coordinating with --.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But I've not stated that they were coordinating with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's self-explanatory, Mr. Jones. Let the witness answer, and then I will see whether he has understood or not. Could you repeat your question, Ms. Sellers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the actions of the soldiers appear to be coordinated and in an efficient manner? Excuse me if the wording isn't exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand. Those were probably soldiers who were well trained, and they entered the village. In my opinion, those were soldiers who were trained to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question, let me put it differently myself. The question is this: Having seen this happening, you, as an eyewitness, did you get the impression that this was a number of men that just happened to be there at the same time, each one going his own way, plundering this or doing that or setting on fire this or setting on fire that, without any coordination between them, or was it a planned, coordinated attack in which they all participated together? This is the question that was put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. They worked in a coordinated manner to carry out an attack and to drive people out, like you have just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, could you now explain to the Trial Chamber what happened next to you during the attack.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Later I came back down from the first floor. My mother -- my wife and my daughter were there. There was little space, because the wounded persons were lying there. And I opened the door and another neighbour came in. Her name was Boznija Damjanovic. It was the third house further south from mine. She approached me and she said she was wounded. I said, "What do you mean wounded, you can still walk." And she held her arm up and she showed me the wound. So I took her back to the house. And she said there was another woman named Vida Lukic who left the house together with her, and Vida was shot and killed on the spot, and she was wounded. So she joined those wounded persons from before, and I put them up in my hallway. There was precious little space there for everyone, so when she came into the house, her son came by to see where his mother was. His name was Slavomir Damjanovic. So he asked me, "Is my mother around? Is she wounded?" And I said, "Yes, but not seriously, she can still move about." And he said, "Can I just go back to my house to fetch something that I left behind?", and I pleaded with him not to go back. It was risky, I said. And he said, "Well they wouldn't let me through, in that case." So I walked him back to his house. The distance is about 30 metres, but we had about -- we had a distance of about 15 or 20 metres to run across. There was a field there. So he went back into his house. He didn't tell me what he would fetch from the house. And then later he told me, I realised what it was all about. He had a key to one of the boats. He wanted to take a boat from the house in order to get his mother across the Drina River and take her across to Serbia to see a doctor. That's what he wanted to do, but he never told me about this. So he went back to his house. I was standing at the corner there. He hardly left the house, heading my way. He fell down, but I didn't hear a single bullet fired. So I was confused. I couldn't actually hear a bullet being fired, but he fell down. And I looked at him, because I was scared. I had to go back to my house. There's another house that was closer, Milan Petrovic's house. I said, "It's probably much safer for me to run to Milan Petrovic's house until the whole situation calms down." I walked into his house and I saw Milan Petrovic's father lying outside the house at the doorstep, and this young man that we called Naser was also lying there, dead. I didn't walk into the house. I ran back to my own house. I was scared. I was tired and exhausted, drained. I didn't know what else to do. That's what I did. But I didn't tell Slavomir's mother that her son had been killed. I simply didn't have the guts to tell her. So I stayed at my house for a while, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rankic, while you were out and going to the house with Slavka, and then coming back in the zig-zag fashion, did you see any village guards shooting at the attackers during that period?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. Everyone had fled and taken cover, so no one knew anything about anyone else. Everyone just looked after themselves. There was no communication. There was heavy shooting but a strange kind of shooting. It was a stop-and-go affair. That's what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to a little bit further in the afternoon or early evening of that same day. Did there come a time period when your wife left the house in order to look for medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Back in my house there were a lot of people, wounded people. There wasn't much space so we were thinking about what to do. I was very tired and exhausted by then, so I asked my wife to go to the house across the way. There was a first aid kit and a man who had a Motorola phone. The idea was for him to call for help, to evacuate the wounded from my house. So my wife ran across the road to that house, and we lost touch until 1900 hours. So I thought that she too had disappeared amid the fire. But at 1900 hours she came back and help arrived, the so-called Red Cross. Some people arrived, quite a number of them, in fact, but the -- the shooting by the Muslim forces had stopped by then. It was quiet and it appeared that the shooting was over. But we still didn't dare leave the house. We just left the house briefly and then go back in. So the Red Cross people arrived, and this man also came over. I can't remember his name. Miroslav Deronjic, he was the one. He came, and some other people. We complained to him and said that he didn't give us any help, and people were killed. And he said that he was not able to send help through to us because there had been an ambush in Voljevica, so that was his excuse, that's what he told us. We picked up the wounded and headed for the Drina. We obtained an authorisation from Yugoslavia allowing us to cross their territory as far as Bratunac, to evacuate the wounded women and children, which is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Thirty-five of us men stayed behind to spend the night and to try to pick up our relatives --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: -- who might have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
