utterances.text: -- yes, I just wanted to clarify some points, okay, for your -- the Trial Chamber. So when Mr. Deronjic came down, are you saying that the villagers explained to him that there had been no reinforcements, no soldiers that came down to assist or defend them during this attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because we sought help via the Motorola phone, but no one came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also, when the evacuation occurred, who was evacuated, and how were they evacuated?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: In the evening, once we had obtained authorisation at 1900 hours from the Yugoslav authorities that we could cross their territory, we used the boats to take the wounded and civilians, women and children, across, across into Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And why didn't you use the road that runs between Bjelovac and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We tried, but there were ambushes along the Bjelovacka Rijeka and towards Zaluzje. People had been wounded there so we had to give up the idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you believe that this was part of a coordinated part of the planned attack, the ambushes that were happening to the north of Bjelovac at the same time as Bjelovac is being attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's what I think too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, did you remain behind with 35 people in the town of Bjelovac that night?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did remain behind. I had a lot of relatives who had been killed, and my aunt, whom I loved very much, she was killed, Obrenja Jankic was her name and she was 60 years old at the time. And it was because of her that I mostly stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the 35 people who stayed behind, did they stay behind to defend the village, or did they stay behind to recover the dead?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We were tired. We had been going for 12 hours. It wasn't a defence any more. We just stayed on to be able to collect our relatives in the morning. And Deronjic said to us -- we didn't want to stay. We said we didn't dare stay because it isn't safe. But he said, "Don't go, stay. There won't be an attack. That was the attack. There won't be another one." Because according to standard practice, that never happened. Things like that didn't happen twice. And he said, "Well, Naser isn't an idiot to make another mistake." That's what he said, that's precisely what that man Deronjic said. "Naser isn't an idiot to make another mistake. He's made one mistake, he won't make another. He's not stupid." So as the man was well-educated himself, this man Deronjic, we were just villagers, we believed him and so we stayed on, the 35 of us, in Dusan Petrovic's house. His was a larger house, a duplex, in fact. So we put up there. Half of us rested up while the other half stood guard and stood watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did some of the people that were in the house, the 35 people, did they come from the village of Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I forgot to say that. Yes. There were people from Sikiric, and they succeeded in escaping and reaching Bjelovac. There were others, on the other hand, from the northern part of Bjelovac who were there. So we all collected there together, we all assembled there, and we told each other what we had seen, what we had experienced, and that kind of thing. They told me, people from Sikiric told me that the Muslim forces first attacked the Loznicka Rijeka, and that they took the river to the Drina River, and that a portion went to the north to Bjelovac, and the rest of them went towards Sikiric. So that's what these people told me, these eyewitnesses who had fled from Sikiric, who managed to escape from Sikiric that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please go back to the map that you have to your right side, and would you please indicate for the Trial Chamber what the men had told you in terms of coming down and then splitting -- going to Sikiric and then to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They said that in order to attack, they took control of the Drina River, one group, whereas the other group went down the Drina River towards Sikiric, whereas the remainder took control of the forest. The forest was free so they took control of it. And we were under siege, completely encircled. We couldn't flee anywhere. And the people that did try to escape were killed. So anybody who tried to escape just didn't manage to succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please mark the place where it appears that the Bosnian Muslim forces split during this attack. On the map, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to put your initials at the angle of the mark that you have put on that map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at the other end, at the other end of the mark. That's one end. Could you put it also at the other end, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Does it go further up, then, or does it stop there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes south and to the north. Two groups; one went to the south, towards Bratunac, and the other group went in a northerly direction, towards Sikiric, along that road, and attacked those houses there, the houses along the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has initialed part of the markings that he has indicated on the map. And from being asked, he explained the direction of the splitting of the group, according to him, being along the -- more or less the Drina River, and the section where, on the map, one can see the words "Vukovicko Polje." Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Rankic, did you learn from the people that were staying in the house that the attack appeared to come from the direction of Pirici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Let me correct that, that the soldiers appeared to come from the direction of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. They used the Loznicka Rijeka, the river, to flow into the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I see. And did you learn from the 35 people who stayed in the house that night that there appeared to be a third force that stayed in the mountains?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would you just indicate on the map for the Trial Chamber where this third force appeared to stay.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness draws a line, a perpendicular line, which comes down from Zaluzje, in the direction of Sikiric, and a little bit further down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And just for clarity, would this third force also be a force that was part of the Bosnian Muslim army? You have to speak.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the firing came from the Drina, and at the same time it would come from the forest, too. And when it stopped from the Drina, it stopped from the forest. And that's how it was, orchestrated, like an orchestra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So in the house that night with the 35 men, did some of those men then help you the next day in terms of picking up the bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: All the people helped. We divided up into three groups. The doctors joined us. And if we found anybody still alive, then we took them to the doctor. And we were divided into three groups. One group went to the north, towards Zaluzje, to pick up those people around the houses, and two groups went towards Sikiric. Just one group went up towards the north, Bjelovac, that is, because there were more people who were killed there. And I was in the group that went towards Sikiric, because my aunt was in Sikiric, so that's why I went that way. And we set off along the road. When we reached Jovanovici, a hamlet, in a ditch we came across a woman called Veseljko Jovanovic. She was middle-aged, and she was the only person who survived. She was wounded in the hip. She wasn't able to move but she was alive. So we took her off to the doctors and we picked up the other bodies and loaded them up onto the tractors, people who had been killed, their bodies. Truth be told, practically all of those had rifles. But when we collected up the bodies, there were no rifles, which meant that the Muslim forces went round picking the weapons straight away. We would come across them in the houses where they were taking out the food from the houses, they were looting food, mostly food, foodstuffs. Some technical appliances, well, but mostly food. That's what we noticed. So we picked up the corpses and took them off and sent them to Grabovica, where there was a boat waiting to transport the bodies to Yugoslavia. We collected them all up and took them to Bratunac, to the health centre there, and they said that they would conduct an examination there. What they did was they took all their clothes off and then conducted those medical examinations or whatever. I don't know exactly. And there were two or three television crews who filmed all this. I'm sure you have the tapes, but if you don't, there are people who can supply you with those tapes. There were 109 bodies, and you can see that 50 per cent of those bodies were people over the age of 50 or younger people, so there were either over 50 or younger people, in Bratunac, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify for the Trial Chamber, are we now talking about December 15th, when the bodies are in Bratunac, when you're describing that over 50 per cent are old people -- older people. I'm trying to pick up his -- I'm near that category too, Your Honour, so I'm sensitive. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you also explain to the Trial Chamber, on the 16th of December, in Bratunac, what occurred with those bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They were transported to the health centre for the post mortems, and their relatives were called in to see if they recognised any of the bodies, to help the doctors, because some of the bodies, the corpses, were in a terrible state. Their faces been blown away by the shells and bombs. So people were called in to assist the doctors. And anybody who had some relatives who had been killed went in to identify the bodies. I went too because there was a young relative of mine, a young guy who had been killed, so that we could see who was who and not mix them up. And on that day, there were 109 corpses. When the doctors counted the bodies, there was 109, and I was an eyewitness to that. There were several issue crews. There was CNN. You couldn't pass by that way. They were busy filming. There were some children of 14 years old there. There was some elderly people, too. So that's what it was, all of them together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, were all of those bodies, just to confirm, were they bodies of people who were Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, they were all people who had died in the attack that took place in Bjelovac and the surrounding areas on December 14th, 1992? All right. And to your knowledge, just to confirm that these bodies were then transported to Bratunac. And were they buried on the 16th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I was present at the time. When they finished the post mortem examinations, it was after 11.00, all the bodies were brought in front of the church in Bratunac for the religious rites to be -- the religious ceremonies take place. We paid our last respects to our relatives and friends, and then we went to the cemetery for the burials. While we were doing that, the others dug the graves so we could get through the burials quickly. We buried the dead, and that was what we did until the evening of the 16th of December. That's what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 17th of December, did you decide to try and go and see what your house looked like in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, as you had to have a permit to go, you couldn't go without a permit, you had to receive a permit from the police. I, and the rest of us who were interested in seeing this -- most people weren't, but I was, because, although my house hadn't been burnt down at that time, Filipovic's house had been burnt and those people, but my house remained intact, and the houses opposite me, on the left-hand side, they were all standing, they were intact. But I received permission, I got a permit to go and see for four hours, and I went to Yugoslavia, in the direction of Grabovac, where I came across a friend who worked in the Radnik company with me. I was a crane operator, and he also worked there. He knew me well. My name is Slavoljub, but they call me Slavko. And he said "Slavko, I saw your house, it was on fire last night." And it was very difficult for me at that point. And then I went up closer, right up to the bank of the river. And as there were some policemen there, the police was there, the Yugoslav police and the army, standing guard at the frontier, the border, I asked hem to lend me their binoculars to have a look. He gave me his binoculars and I could see it, just close up, and yes, my house was burnt down. So I went back and didn't return until March 1993, to Bjelovac. I didn't want to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, about how far were you away from your house in you were in Grabovica and you were looking over the river toward your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, 200 to 250 metres from my house to the Drina River, and then the Drina is 80 metres wide. So that would be it. I got the binoculars. The man lent me his binoculars, and I could see my house very well, very clearly. And all the houses that had been set fire to beforehand, there was smoke coming out of them. I noticed that too, I could see that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So did you notice that there were several houses that were in some stage of burning in Bjelovac on the 17th, when you looked at them from the Grabovica side of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: It depended. If the houses were made of concrete, they burnt down slower. If they were wooden houses or had a lot of wooden elements, they burnt down faster. The people from Grabovac told me that you could see the smoke for several days, until it began raining. So you could see the smoke coming from the houses that were burning, smouldering.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you on what day they noticed that the fires were starting again in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They told us that it was towards evening, or rather, late in the night. Late at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And that would be the night --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- of the 15th, the 16th or the 17th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, when night fell, thereabouts, when it got dark. Before 10.00 p.m., let's say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask now we go to the Prosecution exhibit. I think the number is 432. It's a very short video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it's a video clip, it may raise an issue for us. Is this from the documentary, I wonder, the Uncrowned King of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We object to that video, and I can inform Your Honours why, but I probably should not do this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please escort the witness. We need to discuss something in your absence, a legal argument, before you are shown a video clip, and in the meantime you can have a very short break of about five minutes. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our position as far as this videotape is concerned, The Uncrowned King of Srebrenica, is that this is essentially a Dutch propaganda film, if I may put it that way, which was supplied to the Prosecution by the Dutch Evangelical Church. And that's clear from the ERN 03633610, it's pre-trial exhibit number 385, P425. It originates from the Evangelische Omroep -- I'm sorry, I'll go slowly for the stenographer, who's giving me dirty looks. As Your Honours will be aware, a Dutch battalion was stationed in Srebrenica in July 1995 when the enclave fell, and the Dutch battalion and the Dutch authorities were accused of not doing enough to save the people, Bosnian Muslims, from slaughter by the Serbs. There was an inquiry as a result of which the Dutch government fell in -- on the 16th of April, 2002. It's a major issue, Srebrenica, for the Dutch government, and this film has to be understood - we say as propaganda - in that context. It's designed very much to try and -- to take the blame away from the Dutch and onto our client. And it's full will of inaccuracies which we can show -- we have an extract from the transcript where it's just that, for one example, refers to Slavko Matic, who testified yesterday, as being a teacher, and we know full well from her testimony, that she's not a teacher. She illiterate, according to her. We say semi-literate. We also say there's no way that this video can help this witness with his testimony, and in essence the Prosecution is trying to slip in evidence through the back door by introducing what will probably be interviews with people in order to get that evidence in rather than calling those people as witnesses. You'll see, as I say there, the reference to Slavka Matic being a teacher. So, it's, first of all, patently inaccurate. And secondly, you can even see from this transcript that there are quotations, for example, one has Suljo Hasanovic speaking there, he doesn't speak about Bjelovac, but the Dutch journalist, I'm not sure if it's clear from this extract -- yes, refers to the attack on Bjelovac, and then there's a very brief clip of someone saying something completely out of context, and that being suggested that that relates to Bjelovac, which is entirely -- entirely misleading. One can see the Dutch journalist says "an attack on Bjelovac," then we have Suljo Hasanovic making statements which -- he doesn't mention Bjelovac, so we've got no idea what he's talking about. But there's a caption on the screen saying "attack on Bjelovac." It's -- in our submission, it's a propaganda piece, this documentary, and as I say, coming out of a major -- yes, a -- well, I'm just going to read the selection relating to Slavka Matic. "A teacher, married to Radivoje, two daughters, Gordana and Snezana." And we know -- we know full well she's not a teacher. We are concerned that this trial will be hijacked, as I said in my opening speech, by attempts to use this trial as an exercise in a sort of Dutch political manoeuvre, and that would be, in my respectful submission, would lower the tone of the proceedings at the very least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution certainly would take a bit of offence of being accused of slipping something in the back door using our Prosecution work on behalf of the Dutch government, and doing anything that we think wouldn't be putting through something that we believe is factual and truthful evidence to the Prosecution. More substantively, I think in terms of this video and the source, I really don't know in terms of the religious character of whoever made the video should in any way be an issue at this point. I think we need to look at the veracity of what will be placed before the Trial Chambers, and that this is certainly not under the conditions that we have been discussing here, that we would not to malign any religious group nor any ethnic group within the context of proving facts that relate to allegations and our indictment. I also would like to say that our learned friend's analysis or observations are fruitful in that we do understand some of the critiques that you might have. But as it pertains to this witness, what we have proposed is to show a segment that does not involve any speaking from any of the persons that you have named, that does not involve anything relating to the transcript. We would be -- merely like to show a picture, and almost hold the frame and, as we would any picture that we would present to the Trial Chamber, ask him, does he recognise this picture of this location. This presentation that we are about to do, I think, certainly comes within the bounds of his testimony. He has testified about burning properties. We will show him that segment and ask him whether he recognises it. We will not go into details as to the evangelical nature of the picture, nor anything having to do with the witness that Your Honours was [sic] able to listen to yesterday. And certainly since we do ask the Trial Chamber, "Can we please show this exhibit," we're coming right in the front door and asking, "Can we show an exhibit?", and asking them to be able to rule on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position is we go ahead, we admit this part. For the time being, we are admitting this part of the video clip. We are not interested in the entire video, unless you want to produce the entire video, which you don't seem to be at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that's absolutely correct. Just this one part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And in answer to -- because we are supposed to give a reasoned decision, and this is an oral decision, particularly we considered the submissions made on who provided you with this video, supposedly the Dutch evangelical church, in addition to the fact that it is a Dutch production, to be completely irrelevant at this stage. We're not talking of the events that took place in 1995, but we are talking of the events that allegedly took place in 1993, and particularly the attack on Bjelovac. Mr. Jones himself seems to suggest that there may be a problem in that Bjelovac is being identified in the video clip without, in reality, any ground for that. It's being presumed to be. And for that reason alone, we consider that the testimony of this witness may be crucial, because he should probably be in a position to enlighten us on whether what we see on this video, which we haven't seen, by the way, is indeed the village of Bjelovac or not. Finally, the fact that Slavka Matic is being mentioned here in her capacity as a teacher, which is incorrect, will not really have any bearing on our decision. It is something so marginal that we tend to ignore it. For these reasons, and also on the basis of submissions made by Ms. Sellers, we consider this part of the video clip that we will see as relevant, and we do not consider that the objections raised by the Defence as sufficient -- sufficient to warrant the non-admission of this video clip. So we go ahead. Has this been organised with the technical people or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it's in sanctions, Your Honour. I believe we can bring it up on the video evidence. We've given copies to the registrar and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Judge Brydensholt is drawing my attention, and he is right, that these events allegedly took place in 1993, actually it's 1992. So I'm just saying this for the purpose of the record, and that would correct automatically the transcript. Yes. Whenever you are ready, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask that Mr. Rankic, would you please look at the screen in front of you and tell the Trial Chamber, is this one of the views that you had from Grabovica on the 17th of December, as you looked back into the town of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, can we delete the words and the text that shows under the picture? I mean then they enjoin me in the house where we sat down. I don't know if that's possible, but I don't want to see any words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't seem to be possible. I've asked to see if we can just blacken out the text. The text is in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But those words will not be rolling, it will be static, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: There will be a small rolling. They're in English. My impression is that the witness doesn't understand -- doesn't read the English language. But certainly we're not entering into evidence any of the written text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you increase the size of the picture?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: My case manager informs me that we cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, and then we'll see whether this causes any damage or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, could you answer my question? Do you recognise this scene?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is Stevo Filipovic's house and Slavoljub Filipovic's house, as well as Radovan Vucetic's house. Those houses were, in fact, on fire that day in my neighbourhood, to the right and then south, looking in the direction of my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Where are those houses in relationship to your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They're towards Sikiric, about 100 metres from my house but closer to the Drina River. If you look from the Drina, the distance is about 150 metres from the river, and Slavoljub's house, I think about 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the view of the burning village at Bjelovac similar to what you're seeing today on the video? Was that the view you saw on the 17th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you see other houses in the village that were burning at that time, on December 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These houses, I saw these personally, in front of my house. One of them had a concrete roofing which was cracking, as if under shots that were being fired. But eventually we realised that it was the kind of brick that was used that was to blame for the cracking sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, we can zoom in on that just a tiny bit. I would like to have that done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Rankic, does that assist you in perhaps viewing and making certain that you can identify the houses in that video?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain -- Slavoljub Filipovic's house, Stevo Filipovic's house, and Radovan Vucetic's house, that much I'm certain about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rankic, I have a few more questions for you. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber if any of the Bosnian Serbs who were able to leave the villages of Bjelovac, Sikiric, or the surrounding villages after the attack, were they able to return and live in their villages in that immediate time period after the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't able. They had no where to go. Their houses had burned down. No. Also, for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then my last question is: Did the Bosnian Muslim army, in the aftermath of this attack, reimburse you for the property that you lost in Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I've got nothing for my house. Whoever I talk to, they tell me it just isn't possible. My house sustained a great deal of damage. I did carry out some repairs on my own, but that's not sufficient. There's much more work to be done for years to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rankic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sellers. You're now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Jones. Mr. Jones, you don't need to worry about the Dutch Evangelical Church, because they will not -- they will sleep in peace tonight knowing that they - only this shot was shown out of their video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, your -- and I should say it's not a question of religion; obviously, it's a question of the Dutch authorities I was raising. I wonder whether this is the best place to start or whether we should break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever, I mean I -- no, no, go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you'll give me one moment, Your Honour, so I can get the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, might I -- I'm very sorry, I don't believe I've tendered just this one segment of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't tendered this one and you haven't tendered the map, actually. I was coming to that at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to tender them both. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'd tendered it myself. I had indicated the Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could I tender the map, first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and could I ask the witness to sign that map in some part which is blank and where he could affix his signature. Could you help I am, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour, I would like to tender just that one segment of the video. I think it's been pre-identified as 432, and we would call that small segment here at 432.1, if possible, if the registrar would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it will be. And the other document, the map, I have already confirmed it is Prosecution Exhibit P450. Yes, Mr. Jones, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, first of all, just some general questions about Bjelovac. You've told us that Bjelovac, before the war, was 90 per cent Serb and 10 per cent Muslim. Is it right that then there were about 300 homes in the village, of which about 30 would have been Muslim, before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac only had a handful of families, the ones that I mentioned. I think you're confusing this with Zaluzje, which is adjacent to Bjelovac. That seems to have been an error all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could keep your answers short. I'm not confusing anything, I'm putting questions to you, so if you just answer those. It's right, isn't it, that there were about 60 Muslims in Bjelovac before the war? Wouldn't that be about right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the official statistics. What they said was 10 per cent, but I don't know about the figures. I never checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not asking that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I never asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the statistics. You lived in Bjelovac. I'm asking you: Isn't it right that there were about 60 Muslims living in Bjelovac; do you agree, disagree, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I disagree. Sixty, I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the sake of expediency, I'm not going to put the census being put on the ELMO. I'd propose to just refer Your Honours to Exhibit D82 and it's line 43 on page 72. There's no need to produce it, continuing at line 43 on page 73 for the results of 1991 census, 15 [sic] are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We saw them yesterday anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in Bjelovac, it was suggested to you that people didn't keep crops or have farms. That's not right, is it? There were farmers in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very few, though. Everyone had a house and about an acre of land next to the house. Those weren't large farms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: An acre of land on which most, if not all people grew crops and maybe kept some livestock, just to correct that misapprehension. You were born in Sikiric, and you lived there until you were 26 years old, didn't you? And it's right that in Sikiric, there were more Muslims than Serbs before the war, something like 240 Muslims compared to about 200 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: The Muslims lived in three hamlets, Skela, Laniste and Strzelec. Those were hamlets that were part of Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, for the sake of making progress, I would just refer to Exhibit D82 of the census, line 32 on page 74, continuing at line 32 on page 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 240 Muslims and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We appreciate the approach that you are talking which is very pragmatic and very practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll take your advice, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Sikiric is about 2 or 3 kilometres from Bjelovac, isn't it? I'm sorry, could you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to quickly show you another map, if that could be put on the ELMO. I'm just using that map to put a point to you which perhaps you'll agree with anyway, which is that it's right, isn't it, that Voljevica is actually nearer to Bjelovac than Sikiric, isn't it? Voljevica is really right next door to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No, Zaluzje is. Voljevica is further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could take the pointer and point on the ELMO to Voljevica, and then -- Voljevica, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: This is Voljevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then so Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you see the word Sikiric a little further down from the road?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's where I was born, near the river. This is how far Sikiric extends. That's where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to Voljevica, in Voljevica alone, there were something like 1.375 Muslims before the war, weren't there? Nearly 1.500 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, finally, Your Honours, I will just refer you to the census, D82, line 40, on page 74, going on to page 75, 1.375 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rankic, isn't right that your region -- you don't have to worry about the map for a moment -- that this area, and by that I'm referring to Sase, Sikiric, Voljevica, Biljaca, Bjelovac, Zaluzje, that whole area before the war was mostly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Biljaca, yes; Zaluzje, yes; Voljevica, yes. Ethnically, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've said in an earlier statement to the Prosecutor that the Muslims in Bjelovac left their homes of their own free will in May 1992. Now, is that your -- is that your position, they left of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No one drove them away. They left of their own accord, for reasons of their own safety. Whole families moved out. They went towards Pribici and towards Zaluzje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain those reasons to us. Why would people leave their homes that they've lived in all their lives and everything they have unless they're forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I had a friend named Hajrudin Begzadic. He was a close friend. He came up to me and asked me: What do I stay about that. I told him to stay, and he said he wasn't sure about that. He was afraid the Chetniks would come from Serbia and cut our children's throats. That's what he was afraid of, not his own neighbours, he told me on one occasion. And that's why he moved to Pirici to stay with his brother Mustafa. I knew this man well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that was a legitimate fear, wasn't it? That was something he genuinely had to fear?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, before you proceed, are you making use of this map temporarily, without tendering it as a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. So then we have to enter into the record the following: That the witness was shown a map which the Trial Chamber could see on the monitor, and for the record, when asked to, the witness pointed at the villages or -- the villages of Voljevica, to Zaluzje, and further down to the village of Sikirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us -- you've told us today that the Muslims were provoking you, the Serbs, from the woods. The question I want to ask you, and don't take this flippantly, but the Muslims, they're not monkeys, they're human beings. Do you think they chose to live in the woods when they could live in homes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I don't believe there's been any testimony that they lived in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could help us with that. He told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the question. I think he's understood what is being asked of him.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Muslims are not animals. How shall I put it? Some of them were my friends. Not all, by any means, but some. They went to predominantly Muslim villages. But there were groups that would come over and carry out acts of provocation in the forest, just behind our village. That's all I wanted to say. They didn't live in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But what you did say today is that they couldn't get to their houses. Now, isn't it right that they couldn't get to their houses because Serbs wouldn't let them get to their houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They couldn't get to their houses because there were guards there. That's why they couldn't get through. In daytime, they could have passed through, but not at night, because the guards trusted no one. You know how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your Serb guards were stopping Muslims going back to their homes. You can answer yes or no to the --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: By night.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: By night, no, they couldn't. And by day, yes, they do. No one stopped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've also said that in May 1992, I think you said, that the water supply to Bratunac was cut off by the Muslims in Voljevica. Now, are you saying that the Muslims were still in Voljevica in May 1992, and that they hadn't been expelled by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That's what we were told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown an exhibit which we have. It's a document dated 14th --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: They didn't live there. They just came there to sow some crops.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. This document is dated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To set up ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This document is a letter dated the 4th of July, 2000, from a Mustafa Sacerovic addressed to the Tribunal. There is an ERN number, 03091801. It was used in the Deronjic case, just by way of explanation. And this document refers to expulsions of Muslims from Hranca, Glogova, Bijeceva, Suha. At page 7 it refers to killings in the Vuk Karadzic school. And I would ask Mr. Rankic to turn to page 12 -- sorry, it's 12 in the English. First, to crimes in the villages of Voljevica and Zaluzje, on the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's page 9 of the original, if you have that, Mr. Rankic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is kindly requested to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right, as stated there, that in fact on the 13th of May, 1992, the Bosniak villages of Voljevica and Zaluzje were surrounded by Bratunac SDS paramilitary units, and that Muslim houses were torched, civilians were killed, Muslim civilians? Isn't that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were things like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I direct your attention further down, we see the same Slavko Rankic from Bjelovac, if you stay with the document. It's about five lines from the bottom in your version. It's the last line in our version. Slavko Rankic, and your name there as an SDS supporter who was identified at the scene of the crimes. Now, you've told us that Slavko is a nickname you're known by. That refers to you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: You've made a mistake. I was never a member of the SDS. Even now I am not a member of the SDS. I've been a member of a different party, the SDP. So that's a mistake. That's a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, that's a minor issue. Whether you're in the SDS, it doesn't explicitly say that. It's right --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The scene of ethnic cleansing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No overlap for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll put the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's how we work.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's how we have to move. I think he had arrived at "well, that's a minor issue," and then you continued saying something else, Mr. Jones. I would enjoin you to repeat what you said to the witness after he told you that he had never been a member of the SDS, and then put any question after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Leaving SDS aside, it's right, isn't it, that you were, on the 13th of May, 1992, in Voljevica, in Zaluzje, involved in ethnic cleansing operations against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No, I was never involved in anything like that. I stayed in home all the time. That's where I spent all of my time. I vouch for this with my life, for the truthfulness of my statement. This is a difficult thing for me to face. These are lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't that the reason that you want to hide your face today, not because you wish to prevent your employer from using potential clients?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. As I've explained to the Chamber today -- well, I believe you've heard the explanation, haven't you? What else could it have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you -- I mean, it's a very simple question, and do answer it yes or no. In or on the 13th of May, 1992, when the villages of Voljevica and Zaluzje were allegedly attacked by SDS or Serb paramilitary units, were you there watching what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where were you on that day, when the attack on those two villages took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Bjelovac, in my own village, all the time. I was guarding my own village. I never budged a metre from there. Never, not once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be given a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document is being tendered and -- 89? -- And admitted in evidence and marked as Defence Exhibit D89.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right also, isn't it, that in Sikiric, the Muslims were expelled in the same way; that you've just accepted that Muslims were expelled from Voljevica and Zaluzje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't want to interrupt counsel, but I think he's asking the witness to accept something he hasn't said. I believe that was part of your questions, that the witness said he didn't know anything about it. So I don't mind rephrasing the question, but please don't attribute to the witness that he accepted that this is the manner, according to this document, that crimes occurred. He didn't say ethnic cleansing, he said crimes occurred in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: His answer was very clear, and we're just finding it in the transcript. He accepted that these crimes were occurring, and the crimes which I put to him were of ethnic cleansing. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The transcript may require correction, because I certainly recall the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't recall you asking him to admit that these killings had taken place, but your questions were concentrating on whether these two villages were, indeed, attacked by the Serbs on such and such a day, which resulted with the removal of the Muslims from them. That's -- that was the gist of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may check the tape afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sikiric, the Muslims were expelled from Sikiric in May 1992, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Bratunac as well, it's right, isn't it, that you said in a statement given to the Prosecution, "We returned to Bratunac and were given Muslim homes and apartments to live in because we were refugees." You could take those homes because the Muslims had been expelled, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I said in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I said that in 1993, 1993, when Bjelovac fell, my house had burned down. Where else could I go? I had to live in Bratunac. I was given a house belonging to a Muslim who had left. I don't know how or why. And this was a house that I used, legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've also referred, just before I move on to another subject, to a Mr. Miroslav Deronjic who promised you food and came to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's -- would that be the same Miroslav Deronjic who has been indicted by this Tribunal, if you know, for crimes against humanity, or is it some other Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic, the teacher? Miroslav Deronjic, is that the person you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move on to a question about the village guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the break would normally be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this point we can have a break now, if it's more convenient for you, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a break now -- do you think you'll be able to finish by the end of the sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, Your Honour. The Prosecution has touched on a wide range of subjects. We have video material ourselves to show the witness. We certainly would go into tomorrow, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a break, but we'll resume at 10 minutes past -- 10 minutes past 6.00. Thank you. One moment before we all rise. I take it now that it's too late in the day or in the week to send back the last witness we have on this list -- on the list for this week, that's the one coming on Friday. I'm not going to mention names, because I don't know if there are any protective measures. Is that witness here already?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've been informed that the witness has arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So basically what this entails is that you get together, Defence and Prosecution, and organise yourselves so that between now and the end of business day on Friday, we will finish these two witnesses. I am not curtailing on this witness, because I consider him an important witness, and he's been dealing with very important matters. I don't know about the other two, because I try not to read beforehand as much as I can. But you need to get together and see how you can distribute the time for these two witnesses between you to ensure that both are heard and finished with by the end of the week. Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, the witness appearing tomorrow, Mr. Filipovic, is a material witness, a very important witness for us, and we have lots of documents to show the Trial Chamber in relation to this witness. So regardless of the fact that the OTP have already called a different witness for Friday, can we please have all the time we need for tomorrow's witness, for our cross-examination. He is very important. I will absolutely do whatever is within my power to keep it as brief as possible, but this is not a witness in relation to which we are prepared to make any concessions in terms of length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I want you to get together just the same, see how you can agree on splitting the time, and I'll look into the statements of these two witnesses when I get them. And I will consult with the other two Judges and we'll decide tomorrow morning -- tomorrow afternoon. Break, resuming at 6.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed. Mr. Jones, can I please plead with you to slow down, because I have complaints coming from everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I will, indeed, Your Honour. It's under the pressure to make progress, I think, that made me speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, you've spoken today about the village guard in Bjelovac. In fact, it's right, isn't it, that there was a TO Bjelovac that was part of the Brcanska Brigade commanded by Svetozar Andric long before December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I have no information about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we can show a document, the ERN is 01320384, from the Bratunac collection. That's the first page which says July 1992. And then if the witness can turn over the pages, the page 01320428, we see Bjelovac, or half of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Pausing on that page, I'd like you to look at number 14, Novo Ilic. Is that someone you know from Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Novo Ilic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Son of Stevo. Now, if we keep going, I'll ask you to go to page 01320430, and there we see July 1992. And then the next page, number 37, Slavoljub Rankic. I think that's an N in between. Do you see that? Page 01320431, Slavoljub Rankic: It says "commander to vod".

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's your signature as well, isn't it, further down?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you were actually in an organised unit in Bjelovac --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Village watch, village guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says "commander to vod." Vod is a platoon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you were a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could this document be given a Defence exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I really don't want to interrupt counsel, but I'm just noticing on the document he's handed us, in the translation, it looks like commander was placed to another name, and I just wonder would he clarify that for us. I'm looking at the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: English translation, it is 37, Rankic D Slavoljub, 31, 2nd squad, commander, apart from the wrong spelling of squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. This is what he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think also Mr. Rankic agreed with me that "vod" is a platoon, if that's something he can help us with. Probably not, because it's a linguistic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What were you a commander of? Which platoon were you a commander of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From my house, there were three guard posts stretching over an area of 50 to 100 metres. So in my village, that's where I was, that's where I was standing guard. I was sent to take up my position there, and the others did the same, for defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: You have seen this document, at the end of which is your signature. Did you write this document yourself? Did you compile it yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We compiled these documents to receive food and all the rest of it, so we would keep records like that. To get a sack of flour, a sack of sugar, and oil, vegetable oil. We would write down our names. Otherwise, you wouldn't be given -- issued any food. So these were lists compiled in Bjelovac, not in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just a question with regard to the language. Does "vod" have a special technical meaning, or is it an ambiguous term which could be used for different types of commands? Is it a specialty with regard to military, or are there any other sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it's a military term which I understand is always -- usually translated as platoon, a "ceta" is a company, an "odeljenje" is a section. These are standard terms used in the military in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the whole thing is, does this show that you were part of the army or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said. Just the village guards for the defence, that's what we covered, and that's why we were on guard, and that's what we were doing. Nothing else. If you can understand me, if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were commander of whatever you call it, a village guard or whatever you call it, you were a commander.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: If you have 10 to 12 men standing guard, somebody would have to be there. I would be there for a month, then somebody would replace me. And hundreds of people rotated. You know, we took turns. They were komandirs, not really trained, educated. That was our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Subsequently, you became a soldier in the Bratunac Brigade. Yes. And I'll show another document now with the ERN 0131 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have we given it a number? This is being tendered, this document that has been shown to the witness is being tendered and admitted and marked as D90.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the next document, I was just reading the ERN number, the first page is 01319818, it came from the Bratunac collection. And it's dated October 1992. I would refer the witness to the page which has the ERN 01319822, where one sees Ceta Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it right that there was a company of soldiers in Bjelovac as part of the Bratunac Brigade in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is on page 01319818, and then the next page, Ceta Bjelovac. And I can refer you to the next page, number 663, Slavoljub N. Rankic, "K.Dir ce." That's "commander of ceta," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: It was a replacement. Petrovic Petar was wounded with a sniper. He's a neighbour of mine. So they were supposed to give out food and cigarettes, and I took over from him. That's all. I was still the komandir of the platoon. I was taking over from him because he was wounded, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Petar Petrovic. He was wounded, but with a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You signed this document, did you not, as commander of the ceta. That's your signature at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone can --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Well, everything was written down there. All I know is that I was the komandir of the guard. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can anyone translate or explain to us, under 658, what the words following the name of the person mean, "K.Dir ce," ceta, and then "R forus" [phoen]? Can anyone give me a meaning? Show the document -- the same document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, can you help us with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A few entries above your name, there is the name of the person you mentioned, Petrovic Petar, and then there is "K.Dir ceta," I suppose, and then "R forus." What do those words mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may -- if it assists an English translation, we do have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I tried to look it up. I didn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It should be on the last page, page 3, number 658 is a reserve company commander and reserve lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. A reserve company commander and reserve lieutenant. Do you agree that that's the meaning of those words? What's the "K.Dir ceta"? Does that mean that he's a reserve commander of the brigade, or what? I'm asking you, yes. What do those words mean after Petar Petrovic's name? "K.Dir" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. I never had anything to do with administration, so I'm not quite clear myself. This is all written down here, but I really don't know what all this means, because they wrote this down in the Territorial Defence. Who knows who wrote this. I don't know what they wrote. All I know is that I was on guard, regularly doing my duty. As to the rest of it, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If that could be given an exhibit number, and then we do just have one more document in this series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be D91.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the next exhibit bears ERN 01320783, again from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And my question for you, Mr. Rankic, is: It's right, isn't it, that the Bratunac Brigade was established in November 1992? Could you answer it with words, please, rather than just nodding?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: The 14th of December -- the 14th of November, yes, 1992, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So before the action in Bjelovac, the Bratunac Brigade had been established, and you were a company commander of the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Bjelovac, on -- doing village guard. Just as a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion is my question, the company commander of the 4th Battalion. If you could look at this next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can't go on like this. Question number 1: When was the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade formed, constituted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of November, 1992, was when it was founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you part of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade at any moment since its inception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go out anywhere. We were in Bjelovac all the time. We didn't have any meetings. Mr. Deronjic would come and explain the situation to us, but we didn't leave Bjelovac at all. We were in Bjelovac non-stop, we the defenders of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not answering my question. My question was, and remains: Were you part of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, irrespective of where you were? Were you were enrolled as part of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. The Territorial Defence from Bratunac was the main body. Everything we received was from Bratunac, until the fall of Bjelovac. When Bjelovac fell, then we received, what's it called, the clothes, the booklets, saying that we were part of the army. Up until then, we didn't have any documents, nothing. You know, you could leave whenever you wanted to. Afterwards, you couldn't leave because you'd have to stand a court marshal if you did. That was after the fall of Bjelovac. That's what I remember, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to page -- it's ERN 01320790, the document that's been distributed, it's probably the last page, page 8 in the original, and at the top it says: "4th Ceta, Rankic Nedja, Slavoljub, komandir 4th Ceta."

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: That was written because he didn't come back from hospital, the man Petrovic, Petar Petrovic, so I replaced him the whole time until he came back. So I received a salary. It was all his, you see, I replaced him because I was a soldier without any rank. I wasn't a specialist of any kind. I was, well, one of the engineers. I knew about machines but nothing about rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've finally told us that you were a soldier. In fact, you were a commander from July onwards, weren't you? You were always a commander of some unit, July 1992 onwards. You were a commander of the Bjelovac TO, and now you're a commander of the 4th Ceta, of the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. Isn't that what these documents show?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I'm really not clear on this. All I know was that in Bjelovac, I was the komandir of the village guard. I accept that. As to all the rest of it, I really don't understand it all. How could an ordinary soldier be a company commander, without any training, without any qualifications? Would you take me in as a legal officer without any legal learning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you try and keep your answers short, please, Mr. Rankic. We don't have a huge amount of time, so if you could answer, where you can, yes or no and abstain from lengthy explanations.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know Svetozar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You know him, don't you, because he was the commander of the battalion in which you were. He was your commanding officer. Da.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he your commanding officer? Because you had a number of questions in the same question. Was he your commanding officer, Petrovic, Sreten.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness replied "da," and it wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did come with Deronjic. Now, what he was, I had no idea. He never showed us any documents. He didn't show us any documents so that we know who was what, and there were villagers who didn't recognise him as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could perhaps request at some stage the interpreters listen to the tape. The witness replied "da" when I asked him if Petrovic was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that she thought Defence counsel said "Da." I didn't realise that it was the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said that as well. I can't say that it was the witness. But the thing is I put the question myself, because the question that you put could have confused him, and by answering "Da," he could be answering more than you were asking, actually, Mr. Jones. So that's why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sreten Petrovic was your commanding officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I saw him around. He would come. But how can you know whether someone is a commander if there's no document to bear that out? How can you know who the commander is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the 4th Battalion, which, according to this document, you were in. That was actually based in Sase, wasn't it? It was dealing with the area around Sase, which you mentioned today. It had the zone of responsibility towards Sase. Can you please just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I would see him around. He did come, but I don't know why he came, on what business.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know if it's a problem of translation, but that was nothing like an answer to my question. My question was: Wasn't the 4th Battalion in which you served, did it not have a zone of responsibility towards Sase?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that there was also a 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade covering the Bjelovac-Sikiric area? And if you don't know, you can simply reply, yes, no, or I don't know. There's no need for a lengthy explanation.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I heard him say "nezda," which means "I don't know," and now I see "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was, sir, if you knew that there was also a 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade covering the Bjelovac-Sikiric area. Did you know of the existence of this 2nd Battalion? Yes, no, I don't know? What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because in the meantime you had intervened, and he said Da to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Maybe the witness is speaking to softly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or maybe you are running. Let's proceed slowly. We have enough time. I mean, we will obviously go into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to the page which is marked ERN 01320785. It should be in front of you. There we see "vod minobacaca," with three departments, "odeljenje," underneath. Now, can you tell us what minobacaca stands for, what it is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't know that minobacaca is a mortar-- refers to mortars, and that's a mortar platoon?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you yourself never served in a mortar -- you yourself never served in a mortar unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No. This has been recopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we could show another document from the Bratunac collection. The ERN is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that document. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're tendering it now, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll tender it now and then come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. This will be D92.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this document with ERN 01319928 from the Bratunac collection, if you could turn to 01319940, we there see "vod minobacaca," 82 millimetre, and at 518, Rankic Nedja Slavoljub. Is it right that you did serve in a minobacaca unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The year isn't important, Mr. Rankic. My question is: Did you or did you not serve in a minobacaca unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you saying that this document is -- the information is false?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: This was written by people just to write something down. I had a surgery in my thyroid gland at the time, and my name was on these lists of people who were members of these units just for me have a posting. But I was unable to serve in the military at that time. They were just filling up empty posts. But I'd had a surgery in my thyroid gland at the time, so I was no where at the time. And that's why my name is on these lists, just to keep the posts from being empty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps we can show him also --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: -- and to get the rations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- also show him the signature that appears next to his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he can then tell us whether he recognises it as his own or not, under 518. Perhaps it can be put on the ELMO and enlarged. You have to move it to the left, please. Yes, you have to put the map further up. I will stop you -- I will tell you when to stop. Further up. Stop -- no. Further down, stop. Stop. That last signature which appears to the right of 0554, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, forget about the year. Forget about the year. There are two handwritten pieces there; one says 0554, and then next to it there is the good sign and then a signature. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Rankic, if I understand your evidence correctly, friends of yours, or Serbs in any event, arranged for you to be on these lists so that you could receive money or rations, even though you weren't doing anything at all to earn those rations or that pay; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you surprised, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I'd had a surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: People don't normally get paid for doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: I'd had a surgery. I came back. They can't just -- not for not doing anything. I had to get some rations. I had a wife and two children. I needed food. That's why they put people's names on these lists. This was the case in 90 per cent of the cases. Some were, in fact, working, and some people's names were on the list just for food. And some people tried to get their names in all possible lists, just for the food, just for the rations. This was true of all sides, if you understand my meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the soldiers who were risking their lives were happy for other people to sit back and do nothing and get paid for it; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB RANKIC
utterances.text: We were -- well, I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If that document could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be D93.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to the previous exhibit, and I'd drawn your attention to the minobacaca. Now, you've told us that you weren't interested in matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has a problem. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, we had no mortars whatsoever. That's why I'm surprised where these documents come from. There's no date on any of these. I would love to see a date of issue for these documents. 1992, none whatsoever. That's why I'm surprised, and that's why I'm losing control over everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a date on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think that the witness is tired, we can stop here, Mr. Jones and Ms. Sellers. I don't know what your assessment is. But having heard him say this, I start getting --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. I would want to make clear that there is a document on that -- there is a date on that exhibit, and it's December 1992.
